idiom_name: hand-rolled length-prefixed envelope (POD header + payload bytes)
implementation_notes: C has no message type at all, so the envelope is a struct you define (magic, wire version, message type, payload length) serialized in network byte order with htonl/htons, immediately followed by the payload bytes copied verbatim. Wrap in the outbound adapter and unwrap in the inbound one so the application keeps seeing only its own payload; validate every header field before trusting it - the ntohl-decoded length must be checked against the received buffer size before it indexes anything. RFC 5322's header-section/body split is the classic text instantiation of the same idea; move to a real framing library (protobuf-c, MessagePack, or the transport's own framing) as soon as more than a couple of fields are needed.
pitfalls: Host/network byte-order slips on multi-byte header fields are silent until one architecture meets another; fix the wire order and test both endiannesses.
The length field is attacker-controlled: validate it against the received buffer before any memcpy or pointer arithmetic, otherwise a malformed envelope is a buffer overflow.
The payload tail has no alignment guarantee - do not cast it to a wider type, copy it into an aligned buffer instead.
